title: Fill in the blank: system architecture
prompt: Fill in the missing terms: the parts of a CPU, the clock that paces it, the register that tracks execution, and the marker that starts a comment in GAS.

blanks.prompt: Name the part of the CPU that directs the execution of instructions.
blanks.explanation: A CPU is built from three parts: the control unit, the arithmetic logic unit (ALU), and the registers. The control unit fetches and decodes each instruction, then drives the ALU and the registers to carry it out.
blanks.hint: It does no arithmetic itself, it decides what the other two parts do next.

blanks.prompt: Start a comment at the end of an AArch64 assembly statement.
blanks.code: add x20, x20, x21 ___ accumulate the next term
blanks.explanation: In GAS, // marks the rest of the line as a comment, so a note explaining an instruction can sit beside it. The assembler ignores everything from the marker to the end of the line.
blanks.hint: The same two-character marker that opens a line comment in C++.

blanks.prompt: Name the shape of the signal produced by the system clock.
blanks.explanation: The system clock is a square wave running at a fixed frequency. Its edges pace the processor, so every fetch, decode, and register update is timed against that signal.
blanks.hint: The signal sits at one of two levels and snaps between them, with no gradual ramp.

blanks.prompt: Name the register that holds the address of the instruction being executed.
blanks.code: address of the currently executing instruction = ___
blanks.explanation: The program counter (pc) holds the address of the instruction currently being executed. It is not a general-purpose register: no instruction names it as a source or destination operand, branches change it, adr reads it to form a PC-relative address, and gdb prints it as $pc.
blanks.hint: Every AArch64 instruction is 4 bytes, so this register normally advances by 4.
